correct_feedback: Yes! To compare means to look at two things and see how they are alike and how they are different. Great thinking!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, think about what you do when you hold two things side by side. What are you really checking for?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'find how things are alike and different.' When you compare, you look at two things and notice what matches and what doesn't.

correct_feedback: That's right! A tired dog wants to rest because being tired means it needs sleep. You used the sentence clues well!
incorrect_feedback: Almost! The dog wanted to rest. What kind of feeling makes you want to lie down and stop?
reveal_feedback: The word tired means 'needing sleep or rest.' That's why the dog wanted to rest in the sentence.

correct_feedback: Exactly! A home is the place where an animal lives, just like your home is where you live. Nice job!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. The clue says a home is a place. Which choice tells about a place, not food or fur?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'where it lives.' A home means the place an animal lives, just like the sentence told us.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'The juicy, red apple looked sweet' uses exact words that help you picture it. Describing words make writing come alive!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. Words like 'stuff' and 'thing' are fuzzy. Which sentence paints a clear picture in your mind?
reveal_feedback: The best one is 'The juicy, red apple looked sweet.' It uses exact, describing words so you can really picture the apple.

correct_feedback: Right! Huge means very big, and the elephant was the biggest animal at the zoo. You used the sentence clue perfectly!
incorrect_feedback: Close one! The sentence says the elephant was the biggest animal there. So what does huge tell us about its size?
reveal_feedback: Huge means 'very big.' The sentence even said the elephant was the biggest animal at the zoo.

correct_feedback: Yes! Someone who feels happy feels glad and cheerful. You matched the feeling just right!
incorrect_feedback: Not yet. Think about how your face feels when something wonderful happens. Which words match a happy feeling?
reveal_feedback: Happy means 'glad and cheerful.' Those words describe the good, sunny feeling of being happy.

correct_feedback: Great! 'Ran' is the past-tense of run, so it tells us the race already happened. You picked the right verb!
incorrect_feedback: Almost! You need a verb that shows the race already finished. Say each one aloud and listen for past-tense.
reveal_feedback: The correct sentence is 'My little brother ran fast at the race.' 'Ran' is the past-tense of run, so it shows it already happened.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'The dogs run fast' matches. More than one dog needs the verb 'run,' so they agree. Nice work!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. Check if the naming word is one or many, then see if the verb matches it. Read each one softly.
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'The dogs run fast.' Since there is more than one dog, the verb 'run' matches them correctly.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Faster' compares two things, like one runner is faster than another. You know your comparing words!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, a comparative word compares just two things. Which word adds -er to fast to do that?
reveal_feedback: The comparative form is 'faster.' We add -er to fast when we compare two things.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Happiest' is superlative, meaning the most happy of all. You spotted the top-of-the-list word!
incorrect_feedback: Close one! A superlative shows the most of something out of all. Which word means the MOST happy?
reveal_feedback: The superlative form is 'happiest.' It means the most happy of everyone, more than happier.

correct_feedback: Great! 'I am eating an apple now' is right. 'Am eating' shows it is happening right now. Perfect tense!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. The word 'now' means it is happening this moment. Which verb sounds right for right now?
reveal_feedback: The correct sentence is 'I am eating an apple now.' 'Am eating' shows the action is happening right now.

correct_feedback: Yes! Tom beat Ben, who beat Sara, so Tom is the fastest of all three. You compared them carefully!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. Line them up: Sara, then Ben beat her, then Tom beat Ben. Who ends up on top?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'Tom ran the fastest.' Tom beat Ben, and Ben beat Sara, so Tom is fastest of all three.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Went, saw' are both correct past-tense verbs. The class already went and already saw the paintings. Nice!
incorrect_feedback: Almost! Both blanks happened yesterday, so both verbs need past-tense. Say the pairs aloud and listen carefully.
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'went, saw.' Both are the correct past-tense forms, since the trip happened yesterday.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Because' tells us WHY Mia got so good. It connects her practice to her success. Great choice!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, the question asks which word shows the reason WHY. Which one answers 'why did this happen?'
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'Because.' It shows the reason why Mia became great, since she practiced every day.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Most quietly' means the quietest of everyone, which is why no one could hear him. Well done!
incorrect_feedback: Close one! Jonah was quieter than everyone in the room. Which word shows the MOST out of the whole group?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'most quietly.' Since Jonah was quieter than everyone, we use 'most' to compare him to the whole group.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Went, will go' is right. 'Went' is the past for last summer, 'will go' is the future for next summer. Perfect!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. One blank is about last summer and one is about next summer. Match each verb to its time.
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'went, will go.' 'Went' shows the past for last summer, and 'will go' shows the future for next summer.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Maya said, "Hi!"' puts quotation marks around the exact words Maya spoke. You know your quotes!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. Quotation marks wrap around the exact words a person says out loud. Which one does that best?
reveal_feedback: The correct one is 'Maya said, "Hi!"' The quotation marks go around Hi, the exact word Maya spoke.

correct_feedback: Right! A date needs a comma between the day and the year, like March 5, 2026. Great punctuation eye!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, think about how you write a full date. What small mark goes between the day number and the year?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'a comma between day and year.' We write it March 5, 2026, with a comma before the year.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'I bought apples, bananas, and grapes' uses commas to separate the list. That's just right!
incorrect_feedback: Almost! When you list three things, commas go between the items. Which sentence spaces them out correctly?
reveal_feedback: The correct sentence is 'I bought apples, bananas, and grapes.' Commas separate each item in the list.

correct_feedback: Right! 'The kid's bag' uses an apostrophe to show the bag belongs to the kid. You spotted the owning word!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. To show something belongs to one person, you add a special mark. Which choice has it?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'the kid's bag.' The apostrophe and s show the bag belongs to the kid.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'She said, "hello."' wraps quotation marks around the spoken word and adds a comma. Nicely done!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. The quotation marks go around the exact word she said. Which one also has the right comma?
reveal_feedback: The correct one is 'She said, "hello."' The comma comes after said, and quotes wrap the spoken word hello.

correct_feedback: Yes! '"I found it!" yelled Sam.' keeps the exclamation mark inside the quotes with Sam's exact words. Great eye!
incorrect_feedback: Close one! The exclamation mark belongs inside the quotation marks with the words Sam yelled. Which one does that neatly?
reveal_feedback: The correct one is '"I found it!" yelled Sam.' The exclamation mark stays inside the quotes with Sam's exact words.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Dogs'' shows the tails belong to more than one dog. The apostrophe goes after the s. Well done!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, there are three dogs, so it is many. Where does the apostrophe go when more than one owns something?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'dogs'.' When more than one dog owns the tails, the apostrophe goes after the s.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Its' shows the paws belong to the kitten, with no apostrophe. That's the tricky one, and you got it!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. 'It's' with an apostrophe means 'it is.' Which spelling shows the paws belong to the kitten?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'its' with no apostrophe. It shows the paws belong to the kitten, while it's means it is.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Hopped' doubles the p before adding -ed. That short-vowel rule tripped up others, but not you!
incorrect_feedback: Almost! When a short word like hop ends in one vowel and one consonant, something happens to the last letter before -ed.
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'hopped.' Because hop has a short vowel, we double the p before adding -ed.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'We visited Lake Michigan in July' capitalizes the place name and the month, but not the little words. Perfect!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. Names of places and months start with capital letters, but everyday words do not. Which sentence follows that?
reveal_feedback: The correct one is 'We visited Lake Michigan in July.' Lake Michigan and July are names, so they get capitals.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Fantastic' is the strongest, most exciting way to say good. You picked the powerful word!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, some of these barely mean good at all. Which word sounds the biggest and most exciting?
reveal_feedback: The strongest word is 'fantastic.' It means much more than fine or okay, it means really, really good.

correct_feedback: Right! Writing to a friend, 'Hey, what's up?' is friendly and just the right tone. Good sense of audience!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. You are writing to a friend, not a stranger. Which greeting sounds relaxed and friendly?
reveal_feedback: The best one is 'Hey, what's up?' It's friendly and casual, which fits when you write to a friend.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Strolled' shows a slow, easy walk, so you can picture it. That's a word that paints a picture!
incorrect_feedback: Good try. Most of these just mean go. Which word shows a special way of walking that you can picture?
reveal_feedback: The answer is 'strolled.' It paints a picture of a slow, relaxed walk, more than plain words like went or moved.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Pounced' is a strong verb that shows the cat leaping. It gives you a clear action picture!
incorrect_feedback: Close one! A strong verb shows exciting action you can see. Which cat verb is full of energy?
reveal_feedback: The strongest verb is 'pounced.' It shows the cat leaping with energy, much more than sat or was.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Fierce' shows wind powerful enough to tear off a roof. It matches the strength perfectly!
incorrect_feedback: Hmm, the wind ripped a roof clean off. Which word shows wind that wild and powerful, not gentle?
reveal_feedback: The best word is 'fierce.' It shows wind wild and powerful enough to tear a roof off, unlike chilly or steady.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Thank you for organizing our wonderful field trip' is polite and fits writing to a principal. Great tone!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. You are writing to your principal, so slang doesn't fit. Which sentence sounds polite and respectful?
reveal_feedback: The best one is 'Thank you for organizing our wonderful field trip.' It's polite and respectful, which fits a note to your principal.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Devoured' shows Marco eating fast and hungrily, just right for someone starving. Powerful word choice!
incorrect_feedback: Almost! Marco was starving and ate it in seconds. Which word shows big, hungry, fast eating, not tiny bites?
reveal_feedback: The best word is 'devoured.' It shows fast, hungry eating, which fits Marco who hadn't eaten all day, unlike nibbled or tasted.

correct_feedback: Right! 'Content' is a calm, gentle kind of happy, the mildest of them all. You felt the difference!
incorrect_feedback: Close one! Some of these mean super, super happy. Which word shows the smallest, calmest bit of happiness?
reveal_feedback: The mildest word is 'content.' It means quietly happy and satisfied, much gentler than thrilled or ecstatic.

correct_feedback: Yes! 'Gloomy' gives the house a dark, uneasy feeling, exactly what the author wanted. Great mood match!
incorrect_feedback: Take another look. The author wants readers to feel uneasy and a little scared. Which word gives a dark, spooky feeling?
reveal_feedback: The best word is 'gloomy.' It gives a dark, uneasy feeling, unlike cozy or peaceful, which feel safe and calm.
